title: IN, BETWEEN, and LIKE
summary: Match lists of values, ranges, and text patterns.
intro: Long chains of `OR` and `>=` get hard to read. `IN`, `BETWEEN`, and `LIKE` say the same things in a few words: is it one of these, is it in this range, does it look like this.
setup:
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id integer PRIMARY KEY,
    name text,
    city text,
    email text,
    age integer
);

INSERT INTO customers (id, name, city, email, age) VALUES
    (1, 'Jana Novak', 'Austin', 'jana.novak@Example.com', 34),
    (2, 'Marcus Lee', 'Boston', 'marcus@GMAIL.com', 41),
    (3, 'Priya Shah', 'Denver', 'priya.shah@example.com', 25),
    (4, 'John Carlson', 'Miami', 'JCarlson@gmail.com', 52),
    (5, 'Elena Ruiz', 'Austin', 'elena@outlook.com', 22),
    (6, 'Omar Haddad', 'Seattle', 'omar.h@example.COM', 30),
    (7, 'Jonah Peterson', 'Denver', 'jonah@gmail.com', 40),
    (8, 'Grace Kim', 'Seattle', 'GRACE.KIM@Gmail.com', 50),
    (9, 'Liam Johnson', 'Boston', 'liam.j@example.com', 29);

steps.title: Lists and ranges
steps.body:
Every query in this lesson reads one table, `customers`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (id integer PRIMARY KEY, name text, city text, email text, age integer);
```

```text
 id |    name    |  city  |         email          | age
----+------------+--------+------------------------+-----
  1 | Jana Novak | Austin | jana.novak@Example.com |  34
  2 | Marcus Lee | Boston | marcus@GMAIL.com       |  41
```

It holds 9 customers across Austin, Boston, Denver, Miami, and Seattle.

`IN` checks a value against a list. It is short for a chain of `OR`s:

```sql
WHERE city IN ('Austin', 'Denver')   -- city = 'Austin' OR city = 'Denver'
WHERE city NOT IN ('Boston', 'Miami')
```

`BETWEEN low AND high` checks a range and **includes both ends**, so it means `age >= 25 AND age <= 40`. `NOT BETWEEN` keeps everything outside the range:

```sql
WHERE age BETWEEN 25 AND 40
WHERE age NOT BETWEEN 25 AND 40      -- age < 25 OR age > 40
```

Put the smaller value first. `BETWEEN 40 AND 25` matches nothing, with no error. Both work on text and dates too, like `BETWEEN DATE '2025-01-01' AND DATE '2025-03-31'`.

example.title: Mid-age customers in two cities
example.prompt: List customers in Austin or Denver who are 25 to 40 years old.
example.code:
SELECT id, name, city, age
FROM customers
WHERE city IN ('Austin', 'Denver') AND age BETWEEN 25 AND 40
ORDER BY id;
example.output:
id |      name      |  city  | age
----+----------------+--------+-----
  1 | Jana Novak     | Austin |  34
  3 | Priya Shah     | Denver |  25
  7 | Jonah Peterson | Denver |  40
(3 rows)
example.explanation: `IN ('Austin', 'Denver')` keeps rows whose city is either value. `BETWEEN 25 AND 40` keeps ages from 25 through 40, so Priya (exactly 25) and Jonah (exactly 40) both stay, while Elena (22, Austin) drops out. The first `AND` joins the two conditions, and the one inside `BETWEEN 25 AND 40` belongs to the range.

steps.title: Text patterns
steps.body:
`LIKE` matches text against a pattern. Two characters are wildcards:

- `%` matches any text, including none.
- `_` matches exactly one character.

```sql
WHERE name LIKE 'J%'        -- starts with J
WHERE name LIKE '%son'      -- ends with son
WHERE name LIKE '%an%'      -- contains an anywhere
WHERE city LIKE '_enver'    -- one character, then enver
```

The pattern must match the *whole* value, so `LIKE 'son'` only matches the exact text `son`. Without `%` at an end, that end is pinned.

`LIKE` is case sensitive: `'J%'` misses `jana`. Real data mixes case, especially emails, so use `ILIKE` to ignore letter case:

```sql
WHERE email ILIKE '%@example.com'   -- matches @Example.com and @example.COM
```

`ILIKE` is a PostgreSQL addition, so other databases may not have it.

`NOT LIKE` and `NOT ILIKE` keep the rows that do not match:

```sql
WHERE email NOT ILIKE '%@gmail.com'
```

Only `%` and `_` are special. A `.` is a plain character. To match a real `%` or `_`, put a backslash before it: `LIKE '%\_%'` finds values that contain an underscore.

example.title: J names and example.com emails
example.prompt: List customers whose name starts with J, then customers whose email is at example.com in any letter case.
example.code:
SELECT id, name
FROM customers
WHERE name LIKE 'J%'
ORDER BY id;

SELECT id, email
FROM customers
WHERE email ILIKE '%@example.com'
ORDER BY id;
example.output:
id |      name
----+----------------
  1 | Jana Novak
  4 | John Carlson
  7 | Jonah Peterson
(3 rows)

 id |         email
----+------------------------
  1 | jana.novak@Example.com
  3 | priya.shah@example.com
  6 | omar.h@example.COM
  9 | liam.j@example.com
(4 rows)
example.explanation: `'J%'` means a capital J followed by anything, so it finds Jana, John, and Jonah. The second query uses `ILIKE`, so `'%@example.com'` also matches `@Example.com` and `@example.COM`. With plain `LIKE` only Priya and Liam would match.

practice.prompt:

hints: Put `%` at the start of a pattern so anything can come before the ending you want.
Names are matched case sensitively with `LIKE`. Emails need `ILIKE` because `GMAIL.com` and `gmail.com` should both count.
Leave the end of each pattern without `%`, so an email like `@gmail.com.au` does not match.

recap:
- `x IN (a, b)` matches any value in the list. `NOT IN` matches none of them.
- `BETWEEN low AND high` includes both ends. Put the smaller value first.
- `NOT BETWEEN` keeps values outside the range.
- `LIKE` patterns: `%` is any text, `_` is one character, and the pattern must match the whole value.
- `LIKE` is case sensitive. `ILIKE` ignores letter case.
- `NOT LIKE` and `NOT ILIKE` keep the rows that do not match.
